lessons.title: Scope and object lifetime
lessons.goal: Know exactly when an object is created and when it dies.
explain: Every variable lives inside a scope - the braces it was declared in. It is created when execution reaches the declaration and destroyed when execution leaves that block, always in reverse order of creation.
Returning a local by value is safe because a copy (or a move) leaves the function before the local dies. Returning a reference or pointer to a local is the classic lifetime bug.

example.title: Two lifetimes
notes: an inner block; inner exists only inside it
the value is copied out before local is destroyed
still alive after the block, because it was declared outside

predict.q: In what order are two objects in the same scope destroyed?
options: In the order they were created
predict.why: Destruction is the mirror of construction, so the last created is the first destroyed.

quiz.q: What happens to a local variable when its function returns?
options: It is destroyed; the memory is free for reuse
quiz.why: Its lifetime ends with the scope. Anything still pointing at it is dangling.

quiz.q: Why is returning a reference to a local a bug?
options: The local dies, so the reference points at freed memory
quiz.why: The caller receives a dangling reference and reading it is undefined behaviour - often it even looks correct for a while.

quiz.q: Where do ordinary local variables live?
quiz.why: Automatic variables live on the stack and are cleaned up automatically as the scope exits.

activity.goal: Write a function that returns the square of its argument by value, and print result inside an inner scope.
hints: square returns int and takes one int.
Print result while still inside the braces - outside it no longer exists.
"done" goes after the closing brace.

lessons.mistake: Keeping a pointer or reference to something that has already gone out of scope. If it outlives the object, the pointer is dangling.
lessons.recap: Objects live inside their braces, and die in reverse order when the braces end.

lessons.title: The heap, new and delete
lessons.goal: Create objects whose lifetime you control, and clean them up correctly.
explain: new creates an object on the heap and returns a pointer to it. That object lives until you delete it - it does not care about braces.

Every new needs exactly one delete, and every new[] needs delete[]. Mixing them is undefined behaviour. Forgetting gives a leak; deleting twice is worse. This is why modern C++ rarely calls new directly.

example.title: One object and one array
notes: allocates one int on the heap, value 42
frees it - the pointer still holds the old address
the standard habit: a deleted pointer is set to null

predict.q: What happens if you delete p twice?
options: It deletes the next object too
predict.why: The second delete touches memory that has already been returned to the allocator. Setting the pointer to nullptr after delete prevents the accident.

quiz.q: What does new return?
quiz.why: new allocates and constructs, and hands you the address. Dereference it to use the object.

quiz.q: Which pair matches?
quiz.why: Arrays must be freed with the array form, because the allocator needs to know how many destructors to run.

quiz.q: What is a memory leak?
options: Memory that is allocated and never freed
quiz.why: The program keeps the block reserved until it exits, which matters a lot in a long-running robot or server.

activity.goal: Allocate one int on the heap with value 7, double it through the pointer, print it, then delete it.
hints: int* p = new int(7);
Doubling through the pointer: *p = *p * 2;
delete p; then p = nullptr;

lessons.mistake: Losing the only pointer to a heap object (reassigning it) before deleting it - the object is then unreachable but still allocated.
lessons.recap: new gives you a heap object and the duty to delete it exactly once.

lessons.title: RAII: let the destructor clean up
lessons.goal: Tie a resource's lifetime to an object so it can never be forgotten.
explain: RAII means Resource Acquisition Is Initialisation: acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor. Because destructors run on every path out of a scope - including exceptions - cleanup cannot be skipped.
This one idea is behind std::vector, std::string, std::fstream and every smart pointer. Once you see it, most of C++'s automatic behaviour makes sense.

example.title: A guard that always closes
example.output:
open db
open file
working
close file
end of main
close db
notes: the destructor releases it - automatically, always
close file before end of main
work() ended, so its guard died first

predict.q: If work() threw an exception after creating g, would close file still print?
options: Yes, destructors run while the stack unwinds
Only if you catch it inside work
predict.why: Stack unwinding destroys every fully constructed local object on the way out. That guarantee is exactly why RAII is safe.

quiz.q: What does RAII tie together?
options: A resource's lifetime and an object's lifetime
quiz.why: The object owns the resource, so the resource lives exactly as long as the object.

quiz.q: Which standard library type is RAII?
quiz.why: vector allocates in its constructor and frees in its destructor - the canonical example.

quiz.q: Why is RAII better than writing cleanup at the end of a function?
options: It also runs on early returns and exceptions
quiz.why: Hand-written cleanup is skipped by every early return. The destructor cannot be skipped.

activity.goal: Write a class Timer that prints "start" on construction and "stop" on destruction. Create one in an inner block, then print "after" once the block ends.
hints: The constructor is Timer() and the destructor is ~Timer(), both with a body that prints.
Construct with Timer t; inside the braces.
"after" must be printed after the closing brace so the timer has already died.

lessons.mistake: Writing a destructor that can throw, or forgetting to make a resource-owning class non-copyable - two objects then free the same resource.
lessons.recap: Acquire in the constructor, release in the destructor, and cleanup becomes automatic.

lessons.title: unique_ptr: one clear owner
lessons.goal: Use heap objects without writing delete anywhere.
explain: A std::unique_ptr owns its object and deletes it when it goes out of scope. It cannot be copied - only moved - so exactly one pointer owns the object at any time.
Prefer std::make_unique<T>(args). It is exception-safe and you never write new or delete again.

example.title: One owner, moved once
example.output:
build Five Sides
using Five Sides
build Spare
given away 1
new owner has Five Sides
scrap Five Sides
scrap Spare
notes: constructs on the heap and wraps it in the owner
the pointer syntax still works, same as a raw pointer
destructors run in reverse declaration order

predict.q: Which robot is scrapped first, and why?
options: Spare, because fleet was created first
Five Sides, because moved was declared last and locals die in reverse order
predict.why: Destruction mirrors construction. one, fleet and moved were declared in that order, so moved (holding Five Sides) is destroyed first, then fleet with Spare.

quiz.q: What can you NOT do with a unique_ptr?
quiz.why: Copying would create two owners. Move transfers ownership and leaves the source empty.

quiz.q: Why prefer make_unique over new?
options: It is exception-safe and removes a raw new from your code
quiz.why: With new T(...) passed into a function that then throws, the object can leak. make_unique closes that gap.

quiz.q: What does ptr.reset() do?
options: Deletes the object and makes the pointer empty
quiz.why: reset destroys what it owns, then leaves the pointer null (or takes a new object if you pass one).

activity.goal: Create a unique_ptr<int> with 5, add 3 through it, print it, then reset and print whether it is empty.
hints: auto p = std::make_unique<int>(5);
Dereference like a raw pointer: *p += 3;
p.reset(); then std::cout << (p == nullptr) << "\n";

lessons.mistake: Passing a unique_ptr by value to a function that only needs to use the object - that transfers ownership and empties the caller's pointer. Pass a reference or a raw pointer instead.
lessons.recap: unique_ptr is the default way to own a heap object: one owner, automatic delete.

lessons.title: shared_ptr and weak_ptr
lessons.goal: Share ownership between several places without deciding who deletes.
explain: A shared_ptr keeps a reference count. Copies increase it, destruction decreases it, and the object is deleted when the count reaches zero.
weak_ptr observes without owning. It does not change the count, and lock() gives you a shared_ptr only if the object still exists. Use it to break cycles, which would otherwise never be freed.

example.title: Watching the count
example.output:
count 1
count 2
value 7
count 1
expired 0
expired 1
notes: a copy - the count goes to 2
true once the last owner is gone

predict.q: What would use_count() be after a.reset() if w were the only remaining thing pointing at the object?
options: It would still hold the object
predict.why: Weak pointers observe only. The count reaches 0 and the object is destroyed, which is why w.expired() becomes true.

quiz.q: When is a shared_ptr's object destroyed?
options: When the first pointer goes out of scope
When the last owning pointer is destroyed
quiz.why: The reference count controls it, so the object lives as long as any owner remains.

quiz.q: Why do two shared_ptrs pointing at each other leak?
options: Each keeps the other's count at 1 forever
quiz.why: A cycle keeps both counts above zero. Making one side a weak_ptr breaks it.

quiz.q: What does weak_ptr::lock() return?
options: A shared_ptr that is non-empty only if the object still exists
quiz.why: lock() atomically promotes to a shared_ptr, or returns an empty one if it has expired.

activity.goal: Create a shared_ptr<string>, make a weak_ptr to it, print expired, reset the owner, print expired again.
hints: auto s = std::make_shared<std::string>("Five Sides");
std::weak_ptr<std::string> w = s;
std::cout << w.expired() << "\n"; before and after s.reset();

lessons.mistake: Using shared_ptr everywhere 'to be safe'. Shared ownership makes lifetime hard to reason about; unique_ptr should be your default.
lessons.recap: shared_ptr shares ownership by counting, weak_ptr watches without owning.

lessons.title: Exceptions: reporting the impossible
lessons.goal: Signal failure up the call stack without returning error codes everywhere.
explain: throw starts an exception, which unwinds the stack until a matching catch is found. Objects in between are destroyed properly, which is why RAII and exceptions work well together.
Catch by const reference. Catch the specific type first and a base class like std::exception last. Anything not caught ends the program, so main is a good place for a final catch.

example.title: Parsing three scores
example.output:
ok 88
failed: score out of range: 250
failed: empty score
still running
notes: stops this function immediately - note that nothing after it prints
catches any standard exception by reference
the message carried by the exception

predict.q: What happens to a local RAII object inside parse_score when it throws?
options: Its destructor runs during stack unwinding
predict.why: Unwinding destroys every constructed local on the way out - the guarantee that makes RAII reliable.

quiz.q: Why catch by const reference instead of by value?
options: It avoids slicing and copying the exception object
quiz.why: Catching a base class by value slices off the derived part, so you lose the real type and message.

quiz.q: What ends the program?
options: An exception that reaches main without being caught
quiz.why: If nothing handles it, std::terminate runs and the process aborts.

quiz.q: When should you NOT use an exception?
options: For a file that fails to open
For an expected, ordinary outcome you can check cheaply
quiz.why: Exceptions are for exceptional cases. Ordinary branching (does this key exist?) belongs in the normal control flow.

activity.goal: Write int checked_div(int a, int b) that throws std::invalid_argument when b is 0. Test 10/2 and 10/0, printing ok or the message.
hints: Throw before dividing: if (b == 0) throw std::invalid_argument("divide by zero");
Two separate try blocks, each with its own catch.
Print e.what() in the catch.

lessons.mistake: Throwing a raw pointer or a string literal - catch it somewhere far away and the type will not match. Throw a standard exception type.
lessons.recap: throw unwinds to the nearest matching catch, destroying everything on the way.

lessons.title: std::optional and honest returns
lessons.goal: Return 'a value or nothing' without magic numbers.
explain: std::optional<T> either holds a T or holds nothing. It replaces the sentinel -1, the empty string, and the out-parameter that says whether the call worked.
Check it with if (auto v = f()) or with has_value(), and read with *v or v.value(). value() throws if empty, which is useful when empty really is a bug.

example.title: Looking up a score
notes: an int, or nothing at all
the optional converts to bool: has a value or not
unwraps the value once you know it exists

predict.q: What does *score do if the optional is empty?
options: Undefined behaviour - check first, or use .value_or()
predict.why: operator* does not check. .value() throws std::bad_optional_access, and .value_or(0) supplies a default.

quiz.q: What problem does optional solve?
options: Representing 'no result' without a magic value
quiz.why: It makes absence explicit in the type, so the caller cannot forget it.

quiz.q: How do you get a value or a fallback in one call?
quiz.why: value_or returns the stored value when present, otherwise the argument you passed.

quiz.q: When is optional the wrong tool?
options: When 'nothing' is an error you must not ignore
When the value is a string
quiz.why: optional can be ignored silently. If absence is a real failure, throw or return a result type.

activity.goal: Write std::optional<int> half(int n) that returns n/2 only when n is even, otherwise nullopt. Print half(10) and half(7).
hints: if (n % 2 != 0) return std::nullopt; otherwise return n / 2;
Use if (auto h = half(10)) { std::cout << *h << "\n"; }
The else branch prints "odd".

lessons.mistake: Unwrapping an optional without checking, which turns a missing value into undefined behaviour instead of a clear error.
lessons.recap: optional makes 'maybe nothing' part of the type, so the caller must decide.

lessons.title: Function templates
lessons.goal: Write one function that works for many types.
explain: A template is a recipe the compiler fills in. template <typename T> T bigger(T a, T b) works for int, double, std::string - the compiler generates one function per type you actually use.
The code must compile for each type you call it with. If a type does not support >, the error appears at that call, not at the template.
Deduction is automatic: bigger(3, 9) uses T = int. When two arguments disagree, you must say which type you mean.

example.title: One bigger, four types
notes: T is a placeholder for a type
no copying, whatever the type is
explicit type argument - rarely needed but sometimes clearer

predict.q: What happens if you call bigger(3, 2.5)?
options: It fails to deduce T - the two arguments disagree
predict.why: Deduction needs one consistent T. You must write bigger<double>(3, 2.5) or cast one argument.

quiz.q: When is a template function generated?
options: When it is called with a concrete type
At link time for all types
quiz.why: Templates are instantiated on use, which is why unused ones cost nothing.

quiz.q: Why put the template definition in a header?
options: The compiler needs the body to generate code for each type
quiz.why: Unlike normal functions, the template body must be visible where it is instantiated.

quiz.q: What does a template error usually mean?
options: The template is broken for every type
The body does not work for the type you passed
quiz.why: Templates are only checked per instantiation, so the error names the type that failed.

activity.goal: Write a template T smallest(T a, T b) and use it on two ints (4, 9) and two strings ("kiwi", "apple").
hints: Same shape as bigger, but with < instead of >.
Strings compare alphabetically, which is what you want here.
smallest(std::string("kiwi"), std::string("apple")) forces both arguments to be strings.

lessons.mistake: Putting a template's definition in a .cpp file - other files then fail to link because the body was never visible.
lessons.recap: A template is code the compiler stamps out once per type you actually use.

lessons.title: Class templates
lessons.goal: Build a container type that can hold anything.
explain: A class template makes the type itself generic: Box<int> and Box<std::string> are two different, fully compiled classes produced from one blueprint.
Everything you know about classes still applies - constructors, const methods, encapsulation - the only difference is that T is filled in at the point of use.

example.title: A box that holds anything
notes: the class, with T still unknown
the type is completed at the point of use

predict.q: Can Box<int> and Box<std::string> be stored in the same vector?
options: Yes, they are the same type
predict.why: Each instantiation is a distinct type, exactly like two hand-written classes.

quiz.q: What does the compiler produce for a class template?
options: One class per instantiation you use
quiz.why: Each Box<int>, Box<std::string> is generated separately, which is why unused instantiations cost nothing.

quiz.q: Why is the definition in the header for class templates?
options: Each instantiation needs the body to compile
quiz.why: The compiler must see the members to generate the class for a new T.

quiz.q: What is the standard library's most famous class template?
quiz.why: vector<T> is a class template; cout is an object, and main is a function.

activity.goal: Write a template class Pair<T> holding first and second of type T, with a sum() method returning first + second. Use it with two ints (3, 4) and two strings ("a", "b").
hints: sum() returns T, so first_ + second_ works for numbers and for strings.
Make sum() const.
Construct with Pair<int> p{3, 4}; then print p.sum().

lessons.mistake: Forgetting the <T> at the point of use - writing Box b{3} only works with class template argument deduction, and fails confusingly when it cannot deduce.
lessons.recap: A class template is a blueprint; each type you use creates a real class.

lessons.title: Lambdas and captures
lessons.goal: Write small functions where they are used, and control what they can see.
explain: A lambda is an unnamed function written inline: [](int x) { return x > 3; }. It is perfect for the predicate an algorithm needs and that nobody else will ever call.
The brackets at the front are the capture list. [] sees nothing, [x] copies x, [&x] refers to the original, [=] copies everything used, [&] refers to everything. Prefer naming what you need.

example.title: Two useful captures
notes: a copy of limit - safe even if limit later changes
a reference, so the lambda can modify the original
no capture: it cannot see any local variable

predict.q: What happens if you change limit after the lambda was created with [limit]?
options: The lambda uses the new value
The lambda keeps the value it copied
predict.why: Capture by value copies at the moment of creation. Use [&limit] if you need the live value.

quiz.q: Which capture lets the lambda modify the original variable?
quiz.why: Reference capture reaches the original object; value capture works on a private copy.

quiz.q: Why avoid [&] in something that outlives the current function?
options: The referenced locals are gone, leaving dangling references
quiz.why: A lambda stored for later use must own what it needs, so capture by value.

quiz.q: Can a lambda be stored in a variable?
options: Yes - auto f = [](int x) { return x * 2; };
quiz.why: A lambda is an object with operator(). auto gives it a name, and std::function can hold it generically.

activity.goal: Sort words by length using a lambda comparator, then count how many are longer than 3 letters.
hints: The comparator takes two const std::string& and compares .size().
std::sort(words.begin(), words.end(), [](const std::string& a, const std::string& b) { return a.size() < b.size(); });
count_if with [](const std::string& w) { return w.size() > 3; }

lessons.mistake: Capturing by reference in a lambda that is stored and called later, after the original variable has gone out of scope.
lessons.recap: A lambda is an inline function; its capture list decides what it can see and whether it owns it.

lessons.title: Move semantics
lessons.goal: Understand what std::move actually does and when it saves work.
explain: Copying duplicates the contents; moving transfers them and leaves the source empty. For a big vector or string, moving is O(1) instead of O(n).
std::move does not move anything by itself - it is a cast that says 'treat this as disposable', which lets the move constructor run. A moved-from object is valid but unspecified: do not read it.

example.title: Counting copies and moves
notes: the move constructor - steals, and must not throw
a is still needed, so it copies
a is disposable here, so it moves

predict.q: What is the state of a after Tracker b = std::move(a); ?
options: Valid but unspecified - do not read it
predict.why: The move constructor is allowed to leave a in any valid state. For standard types it is usually empty.

quiz.q: What does std::move(x) return?
quiz.why: It is a cast to T&&. The actual moving happens in the constructor or assignment that receives it.

quiz.q: Why should a move constructor be noexcept?
options: So containers can move instead of copying when they grow
quiz.why: vector only moves elements during reallocation if the move cannot throw - otherwise it copies to keep its strong guarantee.

quiz.q: When is a move automatically used?
options: When returning a local by value, or passing a temporary
quiz.why: Temporaries and returned locals are already rvalues, so the compiler picks the move constructor itself.

activity.goal: Write a class Tag with a copy constructor printing "copy" and a move constructor printing "move". Copy one object, move another, and print "done".
hints: The copy constructor takes const Tag&, the move takes Tag&& noexcept.
Tag b = a; copies, Tag c = std::move(a); moves.
The constructors need no members - just a cout each.

lessons.mistake: Using std::move on a variable you still need afterwards - it is not a hint, it is a promise you are finished with it.
lessons.recap: Moving transfers ownership of the contents; std::move is the cast that allows it.

lessons.title: Project: inventory with tests
lessons.goal: Build a small class with rules, then prove the rules hold with tests.
explain: This project is a stock inventory: it refuses bad quantities, reports totals, and is checked by assertions rather than by printing and eyeballing.
assert is the simplest test: it aborts with a message when the condition is false, and disappears entirely when compiled with NDEBUG. That means tests are free in a release build.

example.title: inventory.cpp
notes: aborts with file and line if false; vanish with NDEBUG
tests the refusal path, not just the happy path

predict.q: If add() accepted qty == 0 instead of throwing, which assert would fail?
predict.why: refused stays false because nothing throws, so assert(refused) aborts. Note the first two asserts would still pass.

quiz.q: What happens to an assert in a build with NDEBUG?
quiz.why: That is why asserts must not contain side effects - the code inside disappears.

quiz.q: Why test the refusal path?
options: Otherwise a bug that silently accepts bad data ships unnoticed
quiz.why: The guard is the feature. Untested guards are the ones that quietly stop working.

quiz.q: What makes this class easy to test?
options: It has no I/O and exposes small queries
quiz.why: Separating logic from output is what lets you assert on results instead of reading text.

activity.goal: Add a remove(item, qty) that throws if the item is missing or the quantity is too large, and assert that a valid removal lowers the total.
hints: Find the entry with a loop over items_ and compare .first.
Throw std::out_of_range if nothing matches, or if qty > entry.second.
Assert total() == 3 after remove("wheel", 1), then print the total.

lessons.mistake: Putting a side effect inside an assert - with NDEBUG the call vanishes and the program changes behaviour between builds.
lessons.recap: Small queries plus asserts turn a class into something you can prove works.
